chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
More and more parents are helping their children access property. It’s a beautiful gesture - one that deserves to be structured to protect everyone. Donation, loan, co-signature: each formula has its implications.

This guide compares ways to help, their benefits and risks, and how to protect yourself.

Informative content, not legal or tax advice: consult a notary and an accountant. Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page.

More and more parents are helping their children access property. This beautiful gesture deserves to be structured. This guide compares ways to help - donation, family loan, co-signing - their benefits, their risks, and how to protect yourself.

Informative content, not legal or tax advice: consult a notary and an accountant.

chapters.title: The donation for the down payment
chapters.html:
Understand the simplest formula.

Donating a sum for a down payment is common and accepted by lenders, provided you provide a donation letter confirming that this is not a repayable loan.

It's simple, but the money donated is no longer yours. Two points of vigilance:

  • Consider theequity between your children (if you have several).
  • Consider the impact on your own retirement finances.

Donation for down payment is common and accepted by lenders, with a donation letter confirming that it is non-refundable. Simple, but the money donated is no longer yours: consider fairness between your children and the impact on your finances. Never empty your retirement cushion to help.

Emilie's advice

Never empty your retirement cushion to help a child. A generous donation that weakens you doesn't help anyone in the long term: help as much as you can really afford.

chapters.title: The family loan
chapters.html:
Lend rather than give, properly.

You can lend rather than giving to your child. In this case, put the terms in writing : amount, reimbursement, possible interest.

Warning: a loan to be repaid can affect borrowing capacity of the child and must be disclosed to the lender.

A poorly documented family loan is a classic source of misunderstandings: clarity protects the relationship.

You can lend rather than give: then put the terms in writing (amount, repayment, possible interest). Please note, a loan to be repaid can reduce the child's borrowing capacity and must be disclosed to the lender. A poorly documented family loan is a classic source of misunderstandings.

Emilie's advice

Put the family loan on paper, even between parent and child. A simple document that specifies “who owes how much, repaid how” avoids years of unspoken words and resentment.

chapters.title: Co-signing: helping without giving money
chapters.objective: Understand the real commitment of a co-signer.
chapters.html:
Understand the real commitment of a co-signer.

In co-signer the mortgage, you help your child qualify thanks to your income and your credit. But the commitment is real:

  • You become responsible for the debt.
  • If the child does not pay, the lender can turn to you.
  • This shows up on your credit report and affects your own borrowing ability.

Co-signing is not a simple courtesy signature: it is a full financial commitment.

By co-signing the mortgage, you help the child qualify with your income and credit - but you become responsible for the debt. If they don't pay, the lender turns to you, and that affects your own borrowing ability. Only co-sign if you can actually afford it.

Emilie's advice

Never co-sign “just to help” without understanding that you are committing to the entire debt. If the child stops paying, the bank will call you. Only sign if you can afford it.

chapters.title: Protect yourself while helping
chapters.objective: Help in a way that protects everyone.
chapters.html:
Help in a way that protects everyone.

Helping your child is a beautiful gesture - which deserves to be structured. A few reflexes protect the child and you:

  • Document systematically (donation letter or loan contract).
  • Consult a notary and a accountant on the legal and tax implications.
  • Plan for the case where the child's couple separates (especially if they buy together).

It's not a lack of trust: it's protecting the family relationship.

Helping deserves to be structured to protect everyone: systematically document it (donation letter or loan contract), consult a notary and an accountant, and plan for the case where the child's couple separates (especially if they buy together). An agreement can protect the amount given.

Emilie's advice

If your child purchases as a couple, consider what happens to your gift in the event of separation. An agreement between spouses can protect the amount you offered. The notary will be able to guide you.

chapters.title: Choosing the right form of help
chapters.html:
Make an informed decision.

Donation, loan, co-signature: each formula has its logic. To choose:

  1. Clarify the form of assistance envisaged and your real capacity.
  2. Evaluateimpact on your own finances.
  3. Document everything (donation letter or loan contract).
  4. Consult a notary/accountant before committing.

Good help is that which helps the child move forward without putting yourself in danger.

Donation, loan, co-signature: each formula has its logic. To choose, clarify the envisaged form and your real capacity, assess the impact on your finances, document, and consult before committing. The right help helps the child move forward without putting yourself in danger.

Emilie's advice

There is no “best” universal formula: it all depends on your situation. The important thing is to choose with full knowledge of the facts, in writing, rather than on impulse.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Clarify the form of assistance envisaged (donation, loan, co-signature).
  2. Assess the impact on my own finances.

Within 30 days

  1. Document the aid (donation letter or loan contract).
  2. Consult a notary/accountant on the implications.

Then

  1. Help in a way that protects the child AND myself.

Before helping

  1. Clarify the form of assistance and assess the impact on my own finances.
  2. Document (donation letter or contract) and consult notary/accountant.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Donation letter: document confirming that a donation is non-refundable.
  • Family loan: repayable aid, to be documented in writing.
  • Co-signature: legal commitment of the parent on the child's mortgage.
  • Borrowing capacity: influenced by a loan to be repaid or a co-signing.
  • Equity between children: to consider when helping only one child.
